name: Sudoku
intro: Learn Sudoku from the rules to real solving techniques: cross-hatching, naked and hidden singles, pencil marks, naked pairs and pointing pairs, with no guessing.

units.name: How Sudoku works
units.blurb: The grid, the boxes and the one rule.

lessons.title: How to play Sudoku: the rules
lessons.summary: Sudoku in one minute: fill the 9×9 grid so every row, column and 3×3 box has the digits 1 to 9 exactly once. Learn by playing.
lessons.wrap: One of each digit in every row, column and box. Next: columns and boxes.

steps.text:
A Sudoku is a 9×9 grid, split into nine 3×3 boxes. Some digits are filled in to start with. They’re called givens.

Your job is to fill every empty cell with a digit from 1 to 9 so that each row, each column and each box contains every digit exactly once.
The thick lines mark the boxes.
steps.prompt: Tap every empty cell in the top-left box.
steps.wrong: Stay inside the top-left 3×3 box, marked by the thick lines.
steps.done: Four empty cells in that box.

steps.text:
Row 2 is almost full. Only one digit from 1 to 9 is missing.

To fill a cell, tap it, then tap a number below the grid.
steps.prompt: Fill the last empty cell in row 2.
steps.wrong: Check which digit from 1 to 9 isn’t in row 2 yet.
steps.done: 3 was the only digit missing from the row.

steps.text: Quick check.
steps.prompt: Can the same digit appear twice in one box?
options: Yes, if they’re in different rows
steps.explain: Never. Every row, column and box has each digit exactly once.

lessons.title: Sudoku basics: columns and boxes
lessons.summary: The Sudoku rule works the same in columns and boxes as in rows. Practise finding the missing digit in a column and in a 3×3 box.
lessons.wrap: Rows, columns and boxes: the same rule three ways. Next: a quick rules check.

steps.text: Columns run from top to bottom. Column 2 has one empty cell left.
steps.prompt: Fill the last cell in column 2.
steps.wrong: Read down column 2. Which digit from 1 to 9 is missing?

steps.text: The same goes for every 3×3 box. The bottom-right box is missing one digit.
steps.wrong: Which digit from 1 to 9 isn’t in the bottom-right box yet?

steps.text: One more.
steps.prompt: In a finished Sudoku, how many times does the digit 7 appear on the whole grid?
steps.explain: Nine times: once in each row, once in each column and once in each box.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Show you know the rules, then on to technique.

lessons.title: Sudoku rules check
lessons.summary: A quick Sudoku rules check: complete a row and answer a question about the rules. Pass it to unlock the solving techniques.
lessons.wrap: Rules done. Now for the techniques that solve real puzzles.

steps.text: Two questions. First, a cell to fill.
steps.prompt: Row 2 has one cell left. Fill it.

steps.text: Second.
steps.prompt: Which of these must contain every digit from 1 to 9?
steps.explain: All three: rows, columns and boxes.

units.name: Solving techniques
units.blurb: Singles, pencil marks, pairs and a routine for any puzzle.

lessons.title: Sudoku technique: cross-hatching
lessons.summary: Cross-hatching is the first Sudoku technique to learn: follow a digit across rows and columns to find the one cell in a box where it fits.
lessons.wrap: Pick a digit, scan the box, cross out the rows and columns. Next: cells with only one possible digit.

steps.text:
Pick a box and a digit it’s missing. The top-middle box has no 6 yet.

Every 6 elsewhere rules out its whole row and column. Cross them out in your head, like hatching lines across the box.
Find the 6s in the rows and columns that cross the top-middle box.
steps.prompt: Put the 6 in the only cell of the top-middle box where it can go.
steps.wrong: That cell shares a row or column with another 6, or isn’t in the top-middle box.
steps.done: The other 6s rule out every other empty cell in the box.

lessons.title: Sudoku technique: naked singles
lessons.summary: A naked single is a Sudoku cell with only one possible digit, because its row, column and box already hold the other eight. Learn to spot one.
lessons.wrap: Count what a cell can see: if eight digits are taken, the ninth goes in. Next: hidden singles.

steps.text:
Look at one empty cell and list the digits already in its row, its column and its box. If that covers eight different digits, the cell can only be the ninth.

That’s a naked single.
The marked cell sees 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 in its row, column and box.
steps.wrong: That digit is already in its row, column or box. Which digit is the only one left?
steps.done: 4 was the only digit left for that cell.

lessons.title: Sudoku technique: hidden singles
lessons.summary: A hidden single is a digit that has only one possible place in a Sudoku row, column or box, even though that cell could hold other digits.
lessons.wrap: Ask “where can this digit go in this row?” as well as “what can go in this cell?”. Next: pencil marks.

steps.text:
Sometimes a cell has several possible digits, but one of them has nowhere else to go in its row, column or box. That’s a hidden single.

Row 3 is missing a 5. Check each empty cell in the row for whether a 5 is allowed.
Most of row 3’s empty cells already see a 5 in their column or box.
steps.prompt: Put the 5 in the only cell of row 3 where it fits.
steps.wrong: That cell sees a 5 in its column or box. Try another cell in row 3.
steps.done: The only place for 5 in row 3, even though that cell could also have been a 1 or a 4.

lessons.title: Sudoku pencil marks: noting the candidates
lessons.summary: Pencil marks are the small digits that list every candidate for a Sudoku cell. Learn how they help you spot singles and pairs in harder puzzles.
lessons.wrap: Notes turn hard puzzles into patterns you can see. Next: naked pairs.

steps.text:
In harder puzzles, write the candidates (the digits a cell could still be) as small pencil marks. The game’s notes button does this.

Here every empty cell shows its candidates.
With notes on, naked singles jump out: a cell with only one small digit.
steps.prompt: Tap the cell in row 3 that has only one candidate.
steps.wrong: Look along row 3 for a cell with a single small digit.
steps.done: Only one candidate: it must be 4.

steps.text: One thing to remember.
steps.prompt: You fill in a 7. Which pencil marks should you update?
options: The 7s in the same row, column and box
steps.explain: Remove 7 from the notes of every cell in the same row, column and box. Those cells can’t be 7 any more.

lessons.title: Sudoku technique: naked pairs
lessons.summary: A naked pair is two Sudoku cells in the same row, column or box with the same two candidates. Learn to use them to clear the rest of the unit.
lessons.wrap: Two cells, two digits: no one else in the unit can have them. Next: pointing pairs.

steps.text:
In row 2, the two marked cells can each only be 1 or 6. One of them is 1 and the other is 6. We don’t know which yet, but those two digits are used up.

So no other cell in row 2 can be 1 or 6. That’s a naked pair.
The outlined cell’s notes say 1, 3 or 6. Take away the pair’s 1 and 6.
steps.wrong: The pair has 1 and 6 covered, so the cell can’t be either.

lessons.title: Sudoku technique: pointing pairs
lessons.summary: Pointing pairs in Sudoku: when a digit’s candidates in a box all sit on one row or column, it can be crossed out of the rest of that line.
lessons.wrap: Box first, then the line it points along. Next: putting it all together.

steps.text:
In the middle-right box, the digit 3 can only go in the two marked cells, and both are on row 5.

Whichever one it is, the box’s 3 is on row 5. So no other cell on row 5 can be 3. The pair points along the row.
The outlined cell on row 5 has candidates 3 and 8.
steps.prompt: Use the pointing pair to fill the outlined cell.
steps.wrong: The box’s 3 must be on row 5 to the right, so this cell can’t be 3.
steps.done: 8. Pointing pairs often unlock a stuck puzzle.

lessons.title: How to solve a Sudoku: a step-by-step routine
lessons.summary: A simple routine for solving any Sudoku: scan for singles, add pencil marks, then look for pairs. Never guess. Learn the order that works.
lessons.wrap: Singles, notes, pairs, never guess. That’s the Sudoku path complete!

steps.text:
Strong solvers follow a routine:

1. Cross-hatch each digit, 1 to 9, through every box.
2. Look for hidden singles in rows and columns.
3. When that dries up, add pencil marks and look for naked singles.
4. Then pairs and pointing pairs, which clear notes and reveal new singles.
Every proper Sudoku has exactly one solution, and it can be reached by logic alone.
steps.prompt: You’re stuck. What should you do?
options: Go back to scanning for singles and pairs with fresh notes
steps.explain: Recheck your notes and look again. A guess that turns out wrong is very hard to undo.

steps.text: Last question.
steps.prompt: Which digits are usually easiest to place first?
options: Digits that already appear many times
steps.explain: A digit that’s already on the grid six or seven times leaves very few places, so cross-hatching finds them fast.
